questions.q: Define "adjective padding" in narrative description and give one example from the story where physical traits are linked to mental qualities.
questions.a: Adjective padding is the accumulation of multiple adjectives or participial phrases before or after a noun to create a dense, layered portrait that simultaneously conveys physical appearance and implied personality. Example: "His mouth, thin-lipped, would tighten in repose to a line that suggested strength of will but might have been only pride." A wrong answer that merely lists adjectives ("tall, thin, near forty") without explaining the physical-psychological linkage reveals the student sees description as decoration rather than characterisation.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the author uses sentence fragments like "The banking establishment of which he had attained control." instead of complete sentences.
questions.a: The fragments mimic the protagonist's wandering, associative memory—his mind jumps from image to image without logical connectives, reflecting shock and dislocation after the bank's collapse. A student who says "it makes the story flow faster" or "it is a grammatical error" misunderstands the stylistic intent: fragments here are a deliberate stream-of-consciousness device, not a mistake or pacing tool.

questions.q: Rewrite the simple sentence "Satyajit felt embarrassed when the women rushed to wash his feet" using the adjective-padding technique seen in the story to show both his physical reaction and inner conflict.
questions.a: "Satyajit, tall, thin, near forty, with sharp features and receding hair shining in patches, shrank back, his smart eye-glasses flashing, the thin line of his mouth tightening not in strength but in a sudden, sharp embarrassment that felt like a betrayal of his former glory." Steps: (1) Identify core fact (embarrassment at feet-washing). (2) Borrow the story's adjective cluster for Satyajit. (3) Add a participial phrase showing physical tell ("smart eye-glasses flashing"). (4) Use a contrastive clause ("not in strength but...") to link body language to inner state. A flat rewrite ("Satyajit, tall and thin, felt embarrassed") misses the psychological layering.

questions.q: Compare the effect of the idiom "Our life-spark itself is held in your fist" with a literal equivalent "Our survival depends on your money." Which better serves the story's theme of false glory? Justify.
questions.a: The idiom wins because "life-spark" and "fist" evoke visceral, almost sacred dependency, framing Satyajit as a deity whose whim decides existence—exactly the "god on the pedestal" illusion the story later shatters. The literal version reduces the relationship to transaction, stripping the irony. A student who picks the literal version for "clarity" misses that the story's central irony *requires* the elevated, metaphorical register to make the fall from glory palpable.

questions.q: Critique the following student claim: "The sentence fragments in the story are grammatically incorrect and should be edited out for formal writing." Provide two textual evidences to refute it.
questions.a: The claim confuses prescriptive grammar with narrative craft. Evidence 1: "The amazing tempo of it all."—a fragment that captures the dizzying speed of Satyajit's rise, impossible to convey in a complete sentence without losing the breathless quality. Evidence 2: "Daughter crisis, indeed!"—a fragment voicing Satyajit's internal sarcasm; expanding it ("It is indeed a daughter crisis") kills the ironic tone. A student who agrees with the claim treats literary grammar as error rather than choice.

questions.q: Create a three-sentence paragraph describing a character's moment of sudden poverty using: (a) one adjective-padded noun phrase, (b) one sentence fragment for interior monologue, and (c) one culturally rooted idiom (Indian or otherwise).
questions.a: Sample: "Ravi, once broad-shouldered and loud-laughed, the man who signed cheques without reading them, stood at the ration queue with a cloth bag trembling in his grip. The empire of his making, dissolved in a monsoon week. His honour was a hollow gourd now, rattling in the wind." (a) "once broad-shouldered and loud-laughed, the man who signed cheques without reading them" (b) "The empire of his making, dissolved in a monsoon week." (c) "honour was a hollow gourd" (rural Indian idiom). A weak answer uses generic adjectives ("poor Ravi"), a complete sentence for the thought, and a cliché ("pride came before a fall").
